info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 10.1: Collaborative Git Workflows for Digital Textual Scholarship.

name.text: 01 Question: The Mid-Term Consolidation Milestone

questiontext.text: What is the primary objective of the Week 10 consolidation milestone in RELS 398?

generalfeedback.text: Consolidation synthesizes nine discrete encoding layers into a shared, multi-editor digital scholarly edition on GitHub.

answer.text: Synthesizing nine accumulated encoding layers into a shared, collaborative digital edition on GitHub.

feedback.text: Correct. Consolidation pauses new tag authoring to connect solitary local workspaces into an integrated, communal edition on GitHub.

answer.text: Discarding earlier diplomatic transcriptions in order to start new documents from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Consolidation preserves and unifies all previous work rather than discarding primary transcriptions.

answer.text: Translating historical documents into modern colloquial English using automated neural models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course focuses on critical digital editing and historical preservation, not replacing source texts with automated translations.

answer.text: Deleting local Git repositories to save hard drive space before final project evaluation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local Git repositories preserve full version history and must be maintained and connected to GitHub.

name.text: 02 Question: From Solitary Editor to Distributed Textual Community

questiontext.text: Why is exchanging manuscript files via email attachments problematic for collaborative digital editions?

generalfeedback.text: Distributed version control replaces chaotic email attachments with a transparent, communal record of all editorial interventions.

answer.text: Files quickly drift out of synchronization, creating untraceable conflicts and losing the rationale behind editorial choices.

feedback.text: Correct. Email attachments lead to version drift, accidental overwriting, and scattered discussions separated from the actual files.

answer.text: Email servers automatically delete all XML files due to international security regulations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Email servers handle XML files normally, but human version management becomes chaotic and unreliable.

answer.text: Email prevents editors from reading primary manuscript facsimiles on high-resolution monitors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Email does not restrict monitor display capabilities; the issue is version drift and lost editorial provenance.

answer.text: Modern XML editors refuse to open any file that has traveled across the Internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors like VS Code open any text file regardless of how it was downloaded.

name.text: 03 Question: The Directed Graph: How Git Tracks Repository History

questiontext.text: How does Git's Directed Acyclic Graph structure protect the integrity of a scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: Git records project history as an immutable graph of commit snapshots, providing permanent citation stability and audit integrity.

answer.text: Each commit has an immutable cryptographic hash based on its contents and parent, making silent retroactive alterations impossible.

feedback.text: Correct. The cryptographic SHA-1 hash incorporates parent pointers and file contents, ensuring that tampering with past commits breaks subsequent history.

answer.text: Git automatically translates archaic French or 18th-century English into modern standardized grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks file snapshots and version history, but it does not alter or modernize textual language.

answer.text: Git encrypts all manuscript images so that unauthorized readers cannot view primary sources.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git records text and metadata history; image access is managed through IIIF and web servers.

answer.text: The graph structure prevents editors from making more than five commits per week.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git places no limits on the number of commits an editor may record.

name.text: 04 Question: The Anatomy of Remotes: Local Clones and GitHub

questiontext.text: In Git version control, what is a "remote repository" such as origin?

generalfeedback.text: A remote repository on GitHub acts as an accessible central anchor for sharing commit snapshots across multiple computers.

answer.text: A copy of the repository hosted on a network server like GitHub that acts as a shared central meeting point.

feedback.text: Correct. A remote repository mirrors your commit graph on the web, enabling synchronization between distributed editors.

answer.text: A specialized hardware cable used to connect two laptop computers directly in a computer lab.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Remotes are software repositories hosted on network servers, not physical cables.

answer.text: An external backup hard drive that is permanently disconnected from the Internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A remote is accessible across the network to facilitate collaborative pushing and fetching.

answer.text: A hidden file on your desktop that stores your operating system passwords.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Remotes are network repository locations, not local password files.

name.text: 05 Question: Collaboration Models: Shared Write Access vs. Fork-and-Pull

questiontext.text: Why does our seminar use the fork-and-pull model rather than granting everyone direct write access to the main repository?

generalfeedback.text: The fork-and-pull model protects the primary edition while inviting outside scholars and peers to propose improvements.

answer.text: It protects the authoritative edition by requiring proposed changes to be inspected, discussed, and validated before merging.

feedback.text: Correct. The fork-and-pull model ensures that all additions are vetted through pull request reviews before entering the master branch.

answer.text: Direct write access causes physical damage to student laptop keyboards during heavy typing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fork-and-pull is an editorial governance strategy, not a hardware protection mechanism.

answer.text: GitHub charges high commercial subscription fees whenever a repository has more than two direct contributors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub provides free collaboration tools for academic and open-source projects.

answer.text: The fork-and-pull model automatically converts TEI XML files into commercial eBook formats.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fork-and-pull governs branch synchronization and peer review; it does not convert file formats.

name.text: 06 Question: Forking a Scholarly Repository on GitHub

questiontext.text: What occurs when you click the "Fork" button on a GitHub repository?

generalfeedback.text: Forking creates a safe personal sandbox where you can freely modify an edition before contributing back to the parent project.

answer.text: GitHub creates a personal duplicate of the entire repository under your account, allowing safe experimentation.

feedback.text: Correct. Forking duplicates files, branches, and commit history into your profile, leaving the upstream project untouched.

answer.text: The original repository is permanently deleted and replaced by an empty folder.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forking never deletes or alters the original upstream repository.

answer.text: All files in the repository are automatically converted into binary executable programs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forking duplicates source text files and version history without altering file types.

answer.text: Your local computer immediately downloads twenty gigabytes of high-resolution print scans.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forking happens on GitHub servers; downloading to your laptop requires a separate clone command.

name.text: 07 Question: Branching Strategies for Digital Scholarly Editions

questiontext.text: Why should editors develop new markup on dedicated feature branches rather than working directly on main?

generalfeedback.text: Isolating editorial work on temporary feature branches keeps the primary main branch clean, stable, and always valid.

answer.text: Working on feature branches keeps the primary main branch clean, stable, and always valid while experiments are underway.

feedback.text: Correct. Feature branches isolate ongoing work, ensuring that incomplete or invalid draft markup never breaks the production text.

answer.text: Git forbids users from creating more than one commit on the main branch per month.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git allows unlimited commits on main, but disciplined editorial practice reserves main for verified stable milestones.

answer.text: Branches automatically compress manuscript image files to save disk space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Branches are lightweight pointers to commits; they do not compress image assets.

answer.text: Working on feature branches eliminates the need to run schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All branches must eventually validate against schemas before merging into main.

name.text: 08 Question: Branch Naming Conventions and Repository Hygiene

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents a well-structured branch name following professional digital humanities conventions?

generalfeedback.text: Meaningful branch names with standard prefixes communicate the exact scope of an editorial task to collaborators.

answer.text: feature/french-named-entities

feedback.text: Correct. Using a standard prefix like `feature/` followed by a concise descriptive summary clearly communicates the scope of work.

answer.text: new-test-branch-final-v2

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generic names like `test` or `final-v2` create confusion about what editorial task is actually underway.

answer.text: stuff_i_did_yesterday

feedback.text: Incorrect. Branch names should identify the textual or technical feature being added, not casual personal timelines.

answer.text: MY_NEW_EDITION_PROJECT!!!

feedback.text: Incorrect. Professional repository hygiene avoids uppercase letters, spaces, and exclamation points.

name.text: 09 Question: Configuring and Managing Remotes via the Command Line

questiontext.text: In a fork-and-pull workflow, what is the role of the upstream remote configured on your laptop?

generalfeedback.text: Configuring both origin and upstream remotes allows your local repository to push personal work and pull shared updates.

answer.text: It allows you to fetch the latest official commits and updates from the primary course repository.

feedback.text: Correct. The upstream remote points to the authoritative central repository so you can keep your local workspace synchronized.

answer.text: It automatically posts your homework grades to your university transcript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Upstream is simply a Git network pointer for fetching repository commits.

answer.text: It deletes your local files whenever you shut down your laptop computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Remotes do not delete local working files.

answer.text: It prevents classmates from viewing your public GitHub profile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Upstream configuration has no effect on user profile visibility settings.

name.text: 10 Question: Synchronizing with Upstream: Fetch, Merge, and Fast-Forward

questiontext.text: What is the key difference between running git fetch and running git merge?

generalfeedback.text: Fetching from upstream and merging into your local main branch keeps your workspace synchronized with project updates.

answer.text: `git fetch` downloads commits without altering your local working files, while `git merge` integrates those commits into your active branch.

feedback.text: Correct. Fetching is safe and non-destructive; merging actively combines downloaded history into your current branch.

answer.text: `git fetch` deletes untracked files, while `git merge` recovers deleted files from the recycle bin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither command deletes untracked files; fetch retrieves remote commits and merge combines branch histories.

answer.text: `git fetch` only works on images, while `git merge` only works on XML documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both commands operate on Git commit graphs regardless of file formats.

answer.text: `git fetch` requires an administrator password, while `git merge` is completely public.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both commands run under standard user permissions in your terminal.

name.text: 11 Question: The Pull Request as the Dynamic Apparatus Criticus

questiontext.text: In what way does a GitHub Pull Request function like a dynamic apparatus criticus in digital editing?

generalfeedback.text: A GitHub Pull Request acts as a living apparatus criticus where editors debate textual readings before adopting them.

answer.text: It serves as a scholarly forum where editors propose readings, cite evidence, and debate textual interpretations before adoption.

feedback.text: Correct. A pull request attaches scholarly rationale and debate directly to proposed markup changes before they enter the master text.

answer.text: It automatically detects and translates Greek and Latin abbreviations without human input.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A pull request is a collaborative review interface, not an automated translation tool.

answer.text: It prints physical paper footnotes along the bottom edge of your laptop monitor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The comparison is conceptual: both provide critical commentary and variant tracking for scholarly scrutiny.

answer.text: It permanently locks the repository against future editorial contributions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pull requests facilitate ongoing contributions rather than locking repositories.

name.text: 12 Question: Anatomy of a Scholarly Pull Request

questiontext.text: Which element is essential in the description of a professional scholarly pull request?

generalfeedback.text: A thorough PR description pairs proposed markup changes with historical evidence, rationale, and schema validation proof.

answer.text: A clear rationale for the changes, accompanied by primary facsimile evidence and schema validation proof.

feedback.text: Correct. A strong PR description explains why changes were made, cites supporting evidence, and confirms that validation checks passed.

answer.text: A generic one-word description like \"fixed\" with no mention of documents or folios.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Vague descriptions force reviewers to guess what was changed and slow down scholarly review.

answer.text: An apology explaining that the XML file contains syntax errors and could not be validated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Authors should fix syntax errors and verify schema compliance before opening a pull request.

answer.text: A list of personal grievances regarding the difficulty of transcribing 18th-century handwriting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PR descriptions should maintain a professional, evidence-based scholarly focus.

name.text: 13 Question: Standardizing Editorial Contributions: `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`

questiontext.text: How does placing `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` in `.github/` improve collaborative edition quality?

generalfeedback.text: Standardized PR templates ensure that every submitted edition update includes required evidence and validation checks.

answer.text: It provides a standard checklist prompting contributors to confirm evidence, authority links, and schema validation before submitting.

feedback.text: Correct. Templates ensure that all authors verify essential criteria like well-formedness, Relax NG checks, and authority records.

answer.text: It automatically rejects any pull request submitted after 5:00 PM on weekdays.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Templates guide human authoring; they do not enforce arbitrary submission curfews.

answer.text: It converts all Markdown text into binary computer code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Templates are plain text Markdown forms displayed in the GitHub browser interface.

answer.text: It removes the need for human peer reviewers to inspect incoming code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Templates assist reviewers by ensuring authors provide necessary contextual evidence up front.

name.text: 14 Question: Visualizing Diffs in Hierarchical XML Documents

questiontext.text: Why is Split Diff view particularly advantageous when reviewing modifications to TEI XML documents?

generalfeedback.text: Using split diff view helps reviewers spot subtle structural changes and mismatched tags in hierarchical XML.

answer.text: It displays original and modified versions side by side, making structural element shifts and unclosed tags immediately obvious.

feedback.text: Correct. Comparing columns side by side reveals structural misalignments and tag omissions that might be obscured in unified view.

answer.text: It translates French and 18th-century English text into modern German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Split diff view compares text versions; it does not perform language translation.

answer.text: It automatically highlights spelling mistakes using red underline animations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Split diff displays textual differences between Git commits, not spell-check alerts.

answer.text: It hides all XML tags so reviewers only read plain unformatted prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reviewing digital editions requires inspecting XML markup tags directly.

name.text: 15 Question: The Scholarly Code Review Interface

questiontext.text: How does GitHub's inline commenting feature facilitate granular peer review?

generalfeedback.text: Inline review comments allow scholars to conduct precise, line-by-line debates directly on the digital text.

answer.text: Reviewers can attach comments directly to specific line numbers in the diff and propose exact XML replacement suggestions.

feedback.text: Correct. Inline comments allow precise discussions tied to specific tags or lines, and suggested changes can be accepted with one click.

answer.text: It sends private text messages to the author's personal mobile telephone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inline comments appear publicly within the pull request thread on GitHub.

answer.text: It prevents authors from replying to reviewer feedback.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inline comments create interactive discussion threads where authors and reviewers debate readings.

answer.text: It deletes any line of text that receives more than two comments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Comments do not delete code; they facilitate scholarly evaluation.

name.text: 16 Question: Iterating on an Open Pull Request

questiontext.text: What should an author do when a peer reviewer suggests revisions on an open pull request?

generalfeedback.text: Pushing new commits to your active branch automatically updates the open pull request, making peer review an iterative cycle.

answer.text: Make the edits on the local feature branch, commit them, and push to GitHub; the PR updates automatically.

feedback.text: Correct. Pushing new commits to the existing branch updates the active pull request without needing to open a new one.

answer.text: Close the pull request, delete the repository, and start the assignment over from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pull requests are designed for iterative improvement; authors simply push corrective commits.

answer.text: Reject the feedback and immediately merge the branch into main without making changes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collaborative editing requires responding constructively to peer feedback and resolving concerns.

answer.text: Email the corrected XML file directly to the instructor as an unversioned attachment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Changes should be committed to Git and pushed to GitHub to preserve public provenance.

name.text: 17 Question: Understanding Merge Conflicts in Hierarchical XML

questiontext.text: Why does Git pause and declare a merge conflict when two branches modify the same line concurrently?

generalfeedback.text: Merge conflicts occur when two branches alter the same lines concurrently; Git safely pauses to let human editors decide.

answer.text: Git cannot determine which scholar's reading is historically or structurally correct and safely asks a human editor to decide.

feedback.text: Correct. Git avoids guessing; when competing edits overlap, it pauses so editors can adjudicate the correct reading.

answer.text: A merge conflict indicates that the user's computer has contracted a dangerous software virus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merge conflicts are standard, expected events in collaborative version control, not virus infections.

answer.text: Git automatically chooses whichever branch was created by the user with more GitHub followers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git does not prioritize users by follower count; it requires explicit human conflict resolution.

answer.text: A merge conflict permanently erases all commit history from both branches.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commit history is completely preserved; only the conflicting lines require resolution.

name.text: 18 Question: Anatomy of a Git Conflict Marker

questiontext.text: In a conflicted file, what text is contained between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`?

generalfeedback.text: Git conflict markers isolate competing readings between HEAD and the incoming branch, requiring manual editing to resolve.

answer.text: The version of the text from your currently checked-out local branch before the merge attempt.

feedback.text: Correct. `HEAD` represents your active local branch, while the incoming branch content sits between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`.

answer.text: The incoming version from the remote branch on GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The incoming version is located between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`.

answer.text: An automated summary of syntax errors generated by the XML parser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conflict markers enclose competing source code lines, not parser error logs.

answer.text: A cryptographic password required to unlock your Git repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conflict markers contain human-readable text from the conflicting commits.

name.text: 19 Question: Modular Architecture and Conflict Mitigation

questiontext.text: How does designing a modular file architecture reduce merge conflicts in a digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Dividing an edition into modular files and assigning clear editorial roles drastically reduces concurrent merge conflicts.

answer.text: Splitting metadata, folios, and entity lists into separate files minimizes concurrent edits on the same lines.

feedback.text: Correct. When editors work in separate modular files (such as distinct folio files or headers), simultaneous line edits rarely collide.

answer.text: It forces all editors to share a single computer terminal in the classroom.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modular architecture enables distributed work across multiple independent computers.

answer.text: It eliminates the need to use XML tags by converting everything to plain text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modular files remain fully encoded TEI XML documents.

answer.text: It prevents Git from tracking file modification dates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks modification timestamps and commit authors across all modular files.

name.text: 20 Question: Step-by-Step Conflict Resolution in VS Code

questiontext.text: Why is choosing \"Accept Current\" or \"Accept Incoming\" often insufficient when resolving conflicts in scholarly editions?

generalfeedback.text: Resolving scholarly conflicts often requires hand-synthesizing complementary markup from both branches rather than picking one.

answer.text: Scholarly conflicts often involve complementary annotations (like one editor adding a lemma and another adding a role) that should be synthesized.

feedback.text: Correct. Blindly picking one version discards the other scholar's valid work; synthesizing both creates a richer, more complete reading.

answer.text: Clicking either button permanently corrupts the operating system registry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The buttons simply accept one text block; the problem is loss of complementary scholarly markup.

answer.text: VS Code disables those buttons for files with a `.xml` extension.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code provides merge conflict buttons for all text files, including XML.

answer.text: Accepting incoming changes deletes the user's local Git repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accepting incoming changes only updates the conflicted text in the working file.

name.text: 21 Question: The Non-Negotiable Step: Verifying XML Well-Formedness

questiontext.text: Why must you always run `xmllint --noout` immediately after editing a conflicted XML file?

generalfeedback.text: Always run xmllint --noout immediately after editing a conflict to ensure no stray markers or broken tags survive.

answer.text: To guarantee that no stray conflict markers or unclosed tags survived, which would cause XML parsers to crash fatally.

feedback.text: Correct. Leftover markers like `<<<<<<<` break XML well-formedness, causing parsers and schemas to abort immediately.

answer.text: To automatically upload the resolved document to the university library archive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `xmllint` is a local syntax checking tool; it does not upload files to archives.

answer.text: To convert British spelling variants into standardized Canadian English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `xmllint` checks XML syntax, not linguistic orthography.

answer.text: To verify that your laptop battery has sufficient charge to complete the commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `xmllint` has nothing to do with battery management.

name.text: 22 Question: Completing the Conflict Merge Commit

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a Git merge commit from a regular commit in repository history?

generalfeedback.text: Staging resolved files with git add and committing creates a two-parent merge commit that reunites diverged branches.

answer.text: A merge commit has two parent commits, joining two diverged lines of development back into a single history.

feedback.text: Correct. Ordinary commits have one parent; merge commits unite two independent branches and record both parents.

answer.text: A merge commit cannot be viewed by other collaborators on GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merge commits are pushed to remotes and viewed like any other commit.

answer.text: A merge commit is automatically deleted after twenty-four hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merge commits are permanent nodes in Git's Directed Acyclic Graph.

answer.text: A merge commit does not require a commit message.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merge commits require clear commit messages documenting how the conflict was resolved.

name.text: 23 Question: GitHub Issues as Scholarly Marginalia and Task Tracking

questiontext.text: How do GitHub Issues function as public scholarly marginalia for digital textual editors?

generalfeedback.text: GitHub Issues serve as public, searchable discussion forums for tracking editorial tasks and resolving paleographical queries.

answer.text: They provide trackable discussion threads where editors discuss paleographical queries, tag collaborators, and preserve research debates.

feedback.text: Correct. Issues serve as a transparent public forum for debating difficult readings, tracking bugs, and assigning editorial tasks.

answer.text: They automatically print physical marginal notes in the margins of original 18th-century manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Issues exist as digital discussion threads on GitHub; they do not alter physical artifacts.

answer.text: They allow students to submit anonymous complaints about course readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Issues are public, attributed project management threads tied to GitHub user accounts.

answer.text: They prevent search engines from finding your digital edition on the web.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Public repository issues are indexed by search engines and contribute to open scholarly transparency.

name.text: 24 Question: Authoring Issue Templates for Digital Editions

questiontext.text: What is the primary benefit of creating specialized issue templates in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`?

generalfeedback.text: Issue templates prompt contributors to provide exact document coordinates, image crops, and competing readings up front.

answer.text: They structure user input with required prompts, ensuring tickets include document coordinates, image evidence, and proposed readings.

feedback.text: Correct. Issue templates prompt users to provide essential scholarly context up front, preventing vague or unhelpful tickets.

answer.text: They allow non-registered users to push code directly to the main branch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Issue templates guide discussion creation; they do not grant code push permissions.

answer.text: They automatically resolve and close all open issues within forty-eight hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Issues remain open until human maintainers inspect and resolve them.

answer.text: They translate all issue discussions into Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Templates display whatever language and fields the repository creators author.

name.text: 25 Question: Project Management: Labels, Milestones, and Kanban Boards

questiontext.text: How do Milestones assist teams in managing collaborative digital edition deadlines?

generalfeedback.text: Labels, milestones, and project boards organize complex editorial labor into clear, trackable collaborative milestones.

answer.text: They group related issues and pull requests together toward a specific calendar target with a visual progress bar.

feedback.text: Correct. Milestones track task completion against a targeted delivery date, showing what percentage of tasks are closed.

answer.text: They automatically deduct points from student grades if an issue is closed late.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Milestones are organizational project tracking tools, not automated grading systems.

answer.text: They prevent collaborators from editing files on weekends or holidays.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Milestones do not restrict editing access times.

answer.text: They delete all open issues once the target date is reached.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open issues remain active until maintainers address them or adjust the target date.

name.text: 26 Question: Case Study: The Scholastic Commentaries and Texts Archive (SCTA)

questiontext.text: How does Jeffrey Witt's SCTA project utilize distributed Git workflows to edit medieval texts?

generalfeedback.text: The SCTA demonstrates how international teams use GitHub repositories and pull requests to edit medieval texts collaboratively.

answer.text: Independent scholars edit Latin commentaries in dedicated Git repositories, which automated scripts aggregate into a shared Linked Data graph.

feedback.text: Correct. The SCTA decentralizes editorial labor across individual GitHub repositories, combining them into a massive unified knowledge base.

answer.text: The SCTA requires all scholars to travel to Paris and work on a single desktop computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The SCTA is an international distributed project coordinating scholars across institutions via Git.

answer.text: The SCTA uses Git exclusively to distribute audio recordings of medieval church music.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The SCTA edits medieval philosophical and theological texts encoded in TEI XML.

answer.text: The SCTA bans pull requests in favor of emailing files on floppy disks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The SCTA relies on GitHub pull requests and automated validation workflows.

name.text: 27 Question: Case Study: Perseids and Classics Collaborative Editing

questiontext.text: What pedagogical innovation does the Perseids Project demonstrate for student textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: The Perseids Project proves that student editors can contribute directly to published digital editions through disciplined version control.

answer.text: Student classroom transcription and treebank annotations are peer-reviewed on Git, merging verified work into the published scholarly record.

feedback.text: Correct. Perseids integrates student coursework directly into authentic, citable digital editions through structured version-control review.

answer.text: Students are graded entirely by artificial intelligence models without any instructor oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Perseids uses human peer review boards modeled on scholarly editorial practices.

answer.text: Students are forbidden from using computers and must complete all work on wax tablets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Perseids is a cutting-edge web platform leveraging digital version control and XML.

answer.text: Student contributions are erased at the end of each semester to protect institutional copyright.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verified student contributions are preserved permanently with proper attribution.

name.text: 28 Question: Case Study: Multimodal Collaborative Editing in E-LAUTE

questiontext.text: What challenge does the E-LAUTE project address using distributed GitHub workflows?

generalfeedback.text: E-LAUTE illustrates how international interdisciplinary teams coordinate complex, multimodal digital editions using Git and GitHub.

answer.text: Coordinating interdisciplinary teams editing multimodal Renaissance artifacts that combine lute music, song lyrics, and visual art.

feedback.text: Correct. E-LAUTE uses GitHub branches, releases, and CI checks to coordinate musicologists, philologists, and programmers across institutions.

answer.text: Translating 20th-century pop songs into ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. E-LAUTE edits 16th-century Renaissance lute tablatures and song texts.

answer.text: Automating the physical manufacturing of wooden musical instruments in factories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. E-LAUTE is a digital scholarly edition project, not a manufacturing enterprise.

answer.text: Banning version control in favor of handwritten letters delivered by courier.

feedback.text: Incorrect. E-LAUTE actively uses GitHub version control and CI pipelines.

name.text: 29 Question: Scholarly Attribution, Provenance, and `<revisionDesc>`

questiontext.text: Why should major Git pull request merges and editorial milestones be recorded in the TEI ``?

generalfeedback.text: Mirroring GitHub pull request merges and milestones inside the TEI revisionDesc element preserves self-contained scholarly provenance.

answer.text: It ensures that the document's internal revision history remains self-contained, citable, and transparent even when offline.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording changes inside `` preserves provenance within the XML file itself, independent of external web platforms.

answer.text: Because Git deletes commit history whenever a repository is cloned to a new computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git preserves full commit history; `` provides standardized internal TEI metadata.

answer.text: Because XML parsers crash if `` contains fewer than ten entries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas do not mandate a specific number of change entries, though historical rigor demands thorough documentation.

answer.text: Because recording revisions in the header automatically increments student grade scores.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Header metadata documents scholarly provenance; it is not a grade tracking tool.

name.text: 30 Question: Looking Ahead to Friday: Preparing for Automated CI and Peer Review

questiontext.text: What preparation is required before Friday's Meeting #27 on Continuous Integration and peer review?

generalfeedback.text: Preparing your repository today sets the stage for Friday's automated GitHub Actions validation and collaborative peer review.

answer.text: Confirming that local witness files contain all nine layers, pass `xmllint` with 0 errors, and are pushed to GitHub main.

feedback.text: Correct. Friday's automated CI and peer review exchange requires a clean, complete, and syntactically valid baseline repository.

answer.text: Deleting all previous commits so that Friday's automated test runs faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version history is essential for peer review; never delete commit history.

answer.text: Printing the entire XML document on physical paper to turn in by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Quality assurance and peer review will be conducted digitally on GitHub.

answer.text: Disabling Internet access on your laptop for the duration of the semester.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GitHub collaboration and CI test runners require Internet connectivity.
